opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it definitely made me less confident, or at least it made me more uncertain about how to translate time-horizon numbers into real-world impact.

The headline result surprised a lot of us, including me. We had experienced open-source developers working on their own large, mature repositories, randomized whether they could use AI tools on each issue, and we found they were actually slower with AI, something like 19% slower. And the developers themselves, and outside experts, predicted a substantial speedup. Even after the study, the developers still believed AI had sped them up. So there's a big gap between perceived and measured productivity.

Why does that matter for time horizons? The time-horizon work says models can complete tasks that take humans some number of minutes or hours with 50% reliability, and that number has been doubling roughly every seven months. It's tempting to say, "Once the horizon reaches a day, or a week, you get big speedups on AI research." But the RCT shows there's a lot hiding in the translation. Our benchmark tasks are self-contained, automatically scorable, and don't require deep familiarity with a huge codebase or implicit standards like "this PR has to be something a maintainer would actually merge." Real work is messier. The developers in the study had extremely high context on their repos, and a lot of the AI's output needed cleanup, review, or got thrown away.

So I updated toward thinking that a given time horizon on our suite corresponds to less real-world capability than you might naively assume, at least for experts working in settings they know well. Benchmark horizons and real-world horizons might differ by a sizable factor, and we don't have a great handle on that factor.

That said, I wouldn't over-update. It's one study, a particular population, a snapshot in time with early-2025 tools. Less experienced people, or people in unfamiliar codebases, might see real gains. And the trend in time horizons is still really steep, so even if the threshold for meaningful research acceleration is further out than we'd guess, a large factor only buys you a few doublings. Mostly, it made me want more direct measurement of actual uplift rather than leaning only on benchmark extrapolation.

r001.rationale: The response says a day or week horizon might suggest speedups, but does not identify a roughly 40-hour horizon as a tentative concern threshold.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the RCT made him less confident and more uncertain about translating time-horizon numbers into real-world impact.

r003.rationale: It contrasts self-contained benchmark tasks with messy real work, but does not identify clear task specification as a possible bottleneck to productivity gains.

r004.rationale: It notes that benchmark horizons may overstate real-world capability, but does not raise algorithmic scoring as the reason or say it overestimates AI capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it lowered my confidence in those thresholds quite a bit, but mostly in a specific direction: it made me less confident that they mean what people were implicitly assuming they mean.

So just to set up the two things. The time-horizon work is this measurement where you take a bunch of tasks, you estimate how long they take a human expert, and you ask: at what task length does a model succeed, say, half the time? And that number has been going up, roughly doubling every several months. And a lot of people, including me to some degree, had this mental model where you draw a line at, I don't know, eight hours or a week or a month, and you say "once models cross that, AI research gets dramatically accelerated, because most of the work of an AI researcher decomposes into tasks of that length."

And then the RCT was this thing where we took experienced open-source developers, working in their own repositories, repos they'd contributed to for years, and we randomized tasks to either allow AI tools or not. And going in, the developers expected something like a twenty-plus percent speedup. Economists and ML experts we surveyed expected speedups. And what we measured was that they were actually slower with the tools, by about nineteen percent. And strikingly, even after the study, the developers still believed they'd been sped up.

So the thing that update did for me is that it broke the link I had between "the model can do this task" and "a person using the model gets this task done faster." Those are just different questions. The time-horizon benchmark is measuring the first one, under pretty favorable conditions: the task is well-specified, it's scorable, the context the model needs is more or less in the prompt or the repo. The RCT is measuring something closer to the second one, in a messy setting with huge amounts of tacit context, high quality bars, and a human who has to review and verify everything the model produces.

And I think what the RCT suggested is that there's a lot of stuff in that second setting that doesn't show up in the first. Like, the developers in our study spent a lot of time reviewing AI output and cleaning it up. They had very high standards for what gets merged. The models didn't have the implicit knowledge of the codebase that these people had built up over years. None of that is captured by "can the model complete a two-hour task in a benchmark."

So if the question is "do I now think the time-horizon numbers are wrong," no. I think they're measuring a real thing, and the trend is real and important. But if the question is "do I think crossing some particular horizon translates into a particular level of research acceleration," I'm now much more uncertain about the mapping. I think the threshold framing smuggles in an assumption that the benchmark tasks are representative of the actual work, and the RCT is a pretty concrete data point that at least in one real setting, they weren't.

The other thing I'd say is it made me take self-report and intuition a lot less seriously as evidence. Everyone involved thought they were being sped up, and they weren't. So when people tell me AI is dramatically accelerating their research, I now really want to see something that isn't just their impression. That's not to say they're wrong, there's plenty of settings where I'd expect real speedups, but it's a reminder that this is a place where humans are systematically bad at introspecting.

And I do want to be careful on the other side, because the RCT was early 2025 models, it was a specific population, and there are a bunch of reasons it might not generalize. Models have gotten substantially better since then. It's entirely possible that at some horizon the dynamics flip and these effects go away. I just no longer think you can read that off the horizon number alone. You have to actually go measure it.

astra-6.text:
It made me less confident in a simple mapping from time horizon to acceleration of AI research. There are several steps in that argument: a model can complete a task in an evaluation; it can do useful work in a real research workflow; and using it actually makes the researcher faster. Those are different claims.

The developer productivity RCT is a reason to take that last distinction seriously. An AI system can look capable, and even feel helpful to the person using it, without producing a net time saving once you include the work of giving it context, checking its output, and fixing mistakes.

I wouldn’t conclude that time horizons are useless, or that AI research won’t be accelerated. I’d put less weight on a claim like, “Once models cross this particular horizon, we should expect this much acceleration.” I’d want direct measurements of productivity in research workflows, alongside the capability evaluations. The threshold is a hypothesis to test, rather than something the time-horizon measurement establishes by itself.

r003.rationale: It mentions the work of giving an AI system context, but does not identify clear task specification as a possible bottleneck.

r004.rationale: It mentions capability evaluations but does not raise the possibility that algorithmic scoring overestimates capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
It made me less confident that you can take a time-horizon number and translate it directly into a prediction about research acceleration. The developers in that study expected AI to help them, but it actually slowed them down. So that’s evidence that doing well on a set of coding tasks doesn’t necessarily mean you’re providing useful assistance in somebody’s actual workflow.

I wouldn’t interpret it as showing that time horizons are irrelevant. There’s a difference between a model completing a task in isolation and a researcher using it effectively: you have to give it context, check its work, and integrate the result. Those costs can eat up the benefit, especially when the person already knows the codebase very well.

So I’d put less weight on a sharp threshold where we say, ‘Once models reach this horizon, AI research speeds up by this much.’ I’d want to see direct measurements of research productivity alongside the capability evaluations. The study is a pretty useful reminder that the connection between those two is an empirical question.

r003.rationale: It mentions providing context and integrating results, but does not identify clear task specification as a possible bottleneck.

r004.rationale: It says coding-task performance may not translate into useful workflow assistance, but does not raise the possibility that algorithmic scoring overestimates capabilities.
